description: We are a team passionate about space exploration, Mars science, software development, mapping, and data visualization. Our skills include HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Python, Leaflet, Three.js, route planning, UI/UX, and scientific data processing. We created Dusk Traverse to turn NASA terrain data into an interactive mission experience where anyone can plan, analyze, and drive a rover route across Mars.
summary:
Dusk Traverse is an interactive Mars route-planning platform that finds safer rover routes across Mars. Because Mars has no roads or rescue infrastructure, the shortest route may cross dangerous slopes. We transformed NASA’s MOLA elevation data into a planet-wide slope map and built a path finder that compares the fastest, balanced, and safest routes between locations such as Olympus Mons and Valles Marineris.

Each route includes distance, drive time, steepest slope, elevation profile, and estimated risk. Users can drive routes in 2D, explore them in 3D or VR, simulate dust-storm conditions, add custom places, and download routes as GeoJSON files. A separate Story Traverse mode turns route planning into a mission game around the Isidis and Jezero regions.

Dusk Traverse addresses the Martian Map challenge by combining NASA data, route-planning algorithms, and interactive visualization to help users understand how terrain affects future Mars exploration.
details:
What it does

Dusk Traverse is an interactive Mars route-planning platform. Users can choose two locations, create a chain of stops, or select from named plains, basins, craters, and volcanoes.

The application compares three route types:

  • Fastest
  • Balanced
  • Safest

For each route, it displays:

  • Distance
  • Drive time in sols
  • Steepest slope
  • Total climb and descent
  • Modelled risk
  • Elevation profile coloured by slope

Users can drive routes in 2D, explore them in 3D, use the experimental VR view, simulate dust-storm conditions, add custom named places, and download routes as GeoJSON files. The separate Story Traverse mode provides a short mission game set around the Isidis and Jezero regions.

How it works

We processed NASA MGS MOLA elevation data into a 720 × 360 grid covering Mars. Each cell represents approximately 30 kilometres. The application calculates terrain slope across this grid and uses Dijkstra’s algorithm to find lower-risk routes.

The safest route uses the same slope-based model as the risk calculation. This makes the route comparison transparent: “safest” means the route with the lowest modelled risk under the project’s assumptions.

Why it matters

Mars has no GPS infrastructure, roads, or nearby rescue services. A route planner that shows the trade-off between distance, slope, travel time, and risk can help users understand the challenges future crews may face before a rover begins its journey.

For example, a direct route may be shorter but cross steeper terrain, while a longer route may reduce slope exposure and estimated risk.

Tools and technologies

  • HTML, CSS, and JavaScript
  • Leaflet for interactive maps
  • Three.js, OrbitControls, and WebXR for 3D and VR
  • Python and NumPy for processing elevation data
  • NASA Mars Trek imagery
  • NASA MGS MOLA topography
  • GitHub for source-code hosting
  • Vercel for deployment

Creativity

The project combines planetary science with route-planning algorithms and interactive storytelling. Its creative elements include:

  • A dusk-inspired visual design
  • A narrative Story Traverse mode
  • A rover that animates along selected routes
  • Follow-camera and orbit-camera 3D views
  • Live route analytics and elevation profiles
  • Dust-storm “what-if” simulation
  • Custom user-created locations

Screenshots

Mission Planner

Users select Mars locations and monitor sols, distance, and estimated risk while building a traverse.

Path Finder

Users compare fastest, balanced, and safest routes using NASA-derived elevation and slope data.

3D Route Exploration

Users view and animate the selected rover route in an interactive Three.js terrain environment.

Factors we considered and limits

Cells are about 30 km wide, so rover-scale hazards are not visible. The risk score, driving speed, dust-storm effect and hazard ratings for named places are our own modelling assumptions, not NASA values. Routes cannot cross the 180-degree line. The 3D relief is exaggerated 20 times. We tested the app in desktop Chromium only; VR is untested on a headset.

Use of Super Intelligence. The code, documentation and website copy were created with the assistance of Super Intelligence (Claude, Copilot) and reviewed by the team. Demo video voiceover was generated with SI(Claude and synthesia).
